Behind the film

How the film was made.

Everything Mosey's film went through, in the order it happened, shown as the things themselves: the plan on paper, the script, the storyboard drafts, the first clips and the ones that failed, every cut, the supercut, the piano, the colours — and what each stage cost. Two days in September, mostly the seventeenth.

4–10 September · a plan on paper

A real shoot, on paper.

Nobody searches the Mac App Store for a walking-pad autopilot, so a listing alone brings no one. One film could carry the site, the store preview, the short clips and the first email to a pad maker. The plan was a live shoot in my own office — the desk fixed, the pad beside it, the laptop carried to a shelf when a call comes — written up as a ticket with the cuts it would need.

The plan, 10 September. One day of filming in my own office — the desk where it is, the pad beside it, the laptop carried to a shelf when a call comes — to get several videos out of one shoot:

  • a thirty-second film for the top of the website;
  • a shorter cut for the Mac App Store, which wants to see mostly the app itself;
  • fifteen- and six-second vertical clips for TikTok and Shorts;
  • a two-minute screen recording to send to a pad maker.

The opening had to be the idea in one image: you get up from the desk and the belt is already moving — an invitation to a walk that has already begun. The words the film had to carry: twenty minutes at the desk, then a walk of three to twenty; and the Blue Zones finding. Captions burned in, because most people would watch it with the sound off.

From the ticket that planned the shoot
17 September, morning · text

Until the shoot: a stand-in, and a script that didn't exist.

On the 16th the idea was to make the film with AI first, following the shoot's script. On the 17th we went to fetch the script and there was none — only an archived narration about villages from an earlier, abandoned film. So the day started with writing it: thirty seconds, six shots, and no voice — the words are cards between the shots.

VIDEO.md, first draft. By the afternoon it had become three parts — why, how, the mechanics — with text cards between the shots.

17 September, midday · images

The storyboard: cents a frame, and the rule it taught.

Every shot was drawn first with an image model, a few cents a frame, and laid on a timeline before any footage was bought. Draft one had four rooms and a man sitting on the pad under the desk. From draft two on, one frame was the reference and every other frame was generated from it — same camera, same furniture. Even then the bookshelf slid across the room five times that afternoon, until the rule: a frame is laid beside its neighbours on a contact sheet and checked item by item before anyone sees it.

≈130 frames · cents each · ≈ €12 for the day
17 September, 15:00 · the first video

The animatic: the whole film, before a cent of footage.

The stills in sequence, each held for its scripted seconds, silent. It cost nothing and settled the timing — “feels good for a first version” — so the clips could be bought against a cut that already worked.

€0
17 September, 15:00 · the words

The cards between the shots.

Silent by default, so the words are cards. The first design was white type on slate, with a black band at the foot; it read like an obituary. The cards moved onto the walks' own colour fields, edge to edge, with the app's type — and that decision came back the next day, when the whole palette changed.

€0 — rendered from the app's own components
17 September, 15:20 · the first clips

The belt that wouldn't move.

The first video model was Google's Veo: eight seconds from a still and a prompt, €2.85 a clip. The walk came out well. The pad waking up did not: in four side-on takes the belt ran the wrong way, a cover slid over it, and once it peeled up like a mat. Shooting it from above with a printed mark on the belt finally moved it the right way — and looked “ugly and technical”. Then the wall: ten generations a day. Nine of the ten clips never made the film.

10 clips · €2.85 · €28.50 — €25.65 of it unused
17 September, 16:45 · a second model

Six seconds for sixty-seven cents.

Kling 3.0 Pro, through a subscription composer first and by API later. The same first frame, side-on: the belt moved the right way on the first try. Every live shot was redone in an hour.

≈35 clips on two ElevenLabs plans ($6 + $22), then 11 by API at $0.67
17 September · the edits

Thirteen cuts in a day.

Every version of the edit, as a filmstrip. The first cuts swap Veo takes in and out; v6 is the first with Kling; v8 and v9 take the notes from watching v7; v12 is the one that became v1.0. Click a strip to see it large.

17 September, 17:30 · a screen inside the film

The call, and a countdown that had to count.

Her screen during the meeting is not footage; it is composed from the app's real menu-bar window over nine generated faces, then animated so the faces move, with the countdown swapped in frame by frame — 0:03, 0:02, 0:01, “Let's walk.”

9 face portraits · cents; 1 clip
17 September, 18:00 · the idea that made the film

The same walk at every hour.

“The same person, same room, at different times of the day, doing different things while walking — a fast-paced cut.” Nine scenarios were drawn, checked on sheets, then generated: a call, a movie, a smoothie, a stretch, a book, a phone. Then sitting at the desk between walks. Then standing. The first four clips cut together were enough: “that supercut is amazing.”

≈30 clips over the evening
17 September, 19:57

v1.0, warts and all.

Fifty-four seconds, silent: the finding, the pad waking on its own, the call with the walk taken along, the walk, the supercut, the card. Everything after this is refinement.

17 September, 20:20 · the soundtrack

“I love Philip Glass.”

A piano piece that starts calm and grows exuberant under the second supercut. Six takes from a music-generation API came back as one texture each — nothing changed at the moments the film changes. Splicing two together was “a mess”. So the piece was written as notes instead: a motif, a bass, a run built from the motif, played by a sampled grand piano. The first written draft threw “random arps and chords at it”; the second was “totally chaotic — go back to reading the scores and start over”; the third went into the film as v2.0, and was then rebuilt some thirty times, one change per render, until the notes fell on the cuts. Each take below with the note it got.

8 generated takes on the subscription; the piano and the synth, free
Generated take 1
I love Philip Glass. Could you figure out a way to use an API to create a song, maybe a piano sonata ‘New York’ that starts calm and becomes more exuberant during the second supercut?
Generated take 3
Every take came back as one texture from start to end — the plan asked for a change at 12 s and at 34 s, and none had one.
Generated take 5
Take 5 does NOT have any change at 12s or at 34s — what are you trying to say here. The piece IS NOT EVOLVING but I asked you several times at this point.
Take 6 — two stems spliced together
Whoa! This is a mess. What did you just do. No. You can't just splice together and increase volume. It should be ONE piece. Maybe you need to simply compose it for real in its entirety and then find a good way to turn those notes into an audio file without AI-gen.
The score, written as notes — what is in the film
SO MUCH BETTER! It's still a bit wonky, especially in the transition from part 2 to 3, and overall the theme isn't there yet — BUT this is a commit and an update of our video online. Consider this v2.0. (Then another twenty-odd passes: the piano's sound, the pauses, one bass note a bar, the cuts on the beat.)
17 September, 21:30 · other people

Other people, at the same desk.

With the API in hand at sixty-seven cents a clip, the room was lent to other people: an older man, an older woman, a student, a man in his middle years — walking, then sitting — and two-person scenes. They joined the supercut, and the cut was put on the beat: every edit a multiple of half a second, two beats a cut in the first round, one in the second.

11 clips · $0.67 · $7.37
18 September · the colours

It looked like a poster for a horror movie.

The next morning, seen all together for the first time — the app, the site, the film — every colour field was a night. A PDF first: the fields as they were, then three looks. Golden hour won. Each walk kept the hues of its own night palette and only the light changed; the cards were re-rendered, the film re-cut. It also cost an afternoon: the re-render was first done at the tools' defaults, which lost the crossfades and doubled the fields' drift, and had to be redone from the exact recipe of the previous cut.

€0 — and one afternoon
the bill

What it cost.

Two days, two people, one of them a model. The money went on generations; the tools that did the rest — the piano samples, the synthesiser, the encoder, the app's own components for the cards and the screens — cost nothing.
